bib.title: Solving Challenging Math Word Problems Using GPT-4 Code Interpreter with Code-based Self-Verification

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Solving Challenging Math Word Problems Using GPT-4 Code Interpreter with Code-based Self-Verification", Zhou, Wang, Lu, Shi, Luo, Qin, Lu, Jia, Song, Zhan, Li (CUHK MMLab et al.). arXiv:2308.07921v1 [cs.CL], 15 Aug 2023. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: 65,615 of 65,615 chars, all 23 pages (body, appendix A.1.1, A.1.2, A.2, example tables). Figures 7/8 (MMLU per-subject charts) are image-only; only their text labels came through. Extraction was clean. No embedded instructions.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Prompting GPT4-Code to verify its answer with code (CSV) lifts MATH accuracy 69.69% to 73.54% on its own; adding verification-guided weighted voting at k=16 reaches 84.32%.
  number: 73.54%, 84.32% (+3.85, +14.63)
  setup: GPT-4 Code Interpreter, zero-shot, full MATH test set (n not stated), 7 subjects; voting k=16 sampled paths, weights wT=1, wU=0.5, wF=0.2.
  quote: "GPT4-Code + CSV ✓ ✗ 56.6 53.9 54.0 85.6 77.3 86.5 86.9 73.54" and "GPT4-Code + CSV + Voting ✓ ✓ (k=16) 74.4 67.8 64.9 94.1 89.0 91.6 95.6 84.32"
  where: Table 1, p.8
- claim: Verifying in natural language does NOT help, while verifying with code does. Same model, same set.
  number: NL verification 69.29 vs. baseline 69.69 (-0.40); code 73.54 (+3.85)
  setup: GPT4-Code on MATH. NL verification fell on 4 of 7 subtopics; code verification rose on all 7.
  quote: "Interpreter Nature Language 52.6 48.7 50.8 79.9 72.5 83.1 82.6 69.29+2.5 -2.8 -2.6 +2.7 +1.9 -3.2 -1.0 -0.40" and "code-based verification enhances accuracy across all 7 subtopics when compared to the Basic Prompt."
  where: Table 4 and Sec 4.4, p.10
- claim: Code-based verification is high precision. Verified-True answers are right about 96% of the time. Recall is lower, so many correct answers are not marked True.
  number: avg precision 95.88%, recall 79.11%, accuracy 73.54%
  setup: GPT4-Code+CSV on MATH, over five sampled paths (Fig 6a).
  quote: "we observed numerical enhancements of 22.3% and 5.6% in the average Precision and Recall, respectively. In particular, the average Precision registered at 95.88%." Fig 6 labels: "Avg. 95.88 Avg. 79.11 Avg. 73.54"
  where: Sec 4.4 p.10; Fig 6 p.11. Appendix: "verification-guided voting is bounded to be effective when the precision of verification is high."
- claim: Weights must rank True above False. If the order is inverted, voting is worse than plain majority voting.
  number: (wT,wU,wF)=(0.5,0.5,1) worse than naive; wT>wU>=wF always beat naive
  setup: MATH, 2 to 16 sampled paths; weight sets 1/0.5/0.2, 1/1/1, 1/0/0, 0.5/0.5/1.
  quote: "When the hyper-parameter setting satisfied wT > wU ≥ wF, the performance of the verification-guided weighted majority voting consistently surpassed that of the naive majority voting methods across all sampled paths."
  where: Sec 4.4, p.10; Fig 6b
- claim: More code use tracks higher accuracy, and the effect grows with problem difficulty. Pilot used code-constrained prompts.
  number: Prompt 2 (code once) beats Prompt 1 (no code) by 6.9 points; Fig 2a shows 60.80, 67.58, 69.94, 74.48 for prompts 1, 2, Basic, CSV
  setup: GPT4-Code on MATH; Code Usage Frequency measured as code executions per problem. Reading of Fig 2a values to prompts is by order, not labelled in the text.
  quote: "Prompt 2 yields an accuracy gain of 6.9 percent over Prompt 1." and "The performance gain when using more code is more obvious in the higher difficulty levels, while in lower levels, the performance gain is not very prominent"
  where: Sec 3.1 p.5; Fig 2 p.5; Sec 4.3 p.9. Correlational (prompts changed, not code use in isolation).
- claim: Self-debugging from execution feedback is part of the base model's strength. Verification adds a check on reasoning and the final answer, which self-debugging does not cover.
  number: none
  quote: "the self-debugging mechanism only verifies each step of the generated code while lacks the verification of the reasoning steps and the final answer"
  where: Intro p.2. Loop formalised as C -> V in {True, False, Uncertain}; False triggers a new solution and re-verification; Uncertain is accepted as final (Sec 3.2 p.6).
- claim: Baseline: GPT4-Code (69.69%) far exceeds GPT-4 without code (42.20%), GPT-4 CoT (50.36%) and PHP (53.90%) on MATH.
  number: 69.69 vs 42.20 / 50.36 / 53.90
  setup: MATH, table 1; baselines are as the authors report them.
  quote: "GPT-4 (PHP) ✗ ✗ 26.3 29.8 41.9 55.7 56.3 73.8 74.3 53.90"
  where: Table 1, p.8
- claim: Other benchmarks improve less, because the base is already strong.
  number: GSM8K 92.9 to 97.0 (5 paths); MMLU-Math 87.5 to 89.2; MMLU-STEM 86.8 to 87.0
  setup: GPT4-Code zero-shot, CSV + voting. GSM8K comparison rows: GPT-4 PHP 96.5 (40 paths), GPT-4 model selection 96.8 (15 paths).
  quote: "GPT4-Code + CSV + Voting 5 97.0"; "GPT4-Code Math 87.5 zero-shot"; "GPT4-Code + CSV + Voting Math 89.2 zero-shot"; "GPT4-Code + CSV + Voting STEM 87.0 zero-shot"
  where: Tables 2-3, p.9
- claim: Gains by subject are uneven. Geometry gains only 0.6 points from CSV.
  number: +0.6 (Geometry), +7.6/+8.4 (Number Theory; Table 1 prints +7.6, Table 4 prints +8.4 for the same 77.2 to 85.6)
  setup: MATH subtopics. Authors guess the cause is that geometry needs multimodality.
  quote: "the Geometry problem only has an increased accuracy of 0.6%"
  where: Sec 4.1 p.8. Internal inconsistency flagged in PROBLEMS.
- claim: sympy dominates the code the model writes.
  number: sympy 0.4168 per problem, math 0.1590
  quote: "the sympy package is utilized most frequently"
  where: Table 6, p.15

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "our analysis and improvements are currently focused on GPT4-Code, which is somewhat restrictive." Other LLMs not tested. Open-source fine-tuning is untested future work.
- Closed model with a built-in code sandbox; results depend on that product version (August 2023, since superseded). The authors say the high result "is based on the strong abilities of the base model."
- Verification is the model grading its own answer. The paper does not separate "verification catches errors" from "extra code or longer reasoning helps".
- The paper reports no variance, seeds, confidence intervals or number of samples. Test-set size is not stated.
- Voting weights were chosen by the authors with ablation on the same benchmark; no held-out tuning is described.
- The Uncertain state is accepted as final, and the paper does not report how often it occurs.
- Math answers have a checkable computation; the paper does not show transfer to tasks without a computable check.
- Appendix example Table 12 shows a verification that wrongly passed or failed (True succeeds while Uncertain and False fail on a correct answer), so verification can mislead.

BUILDS ON: Wei et al. 2022 (CoT); Kojima et al. 2022 (zero-shot CoT); Wang et al. 2023 (self-consistency, majority voting); Gao et al. 2023 (PAL); Chen et al. 2022 (PoT); Cobbe et al. 2021 (trained verifiers, GSM8K); Lightman et al. 2023 (Let's verify step by step); Weng et al. 2023 (LLM self-verification); Madaan et al. 2023 (Self-Refine); Zheng et al. 2023 (PHP, the previous SOTA at 53.9%); Zhao et al. 2023 (model selection).

CODE: The CSV prompt, verbatim: "To solve the problem using code interpreter step by step, and please verify your answer using code interpreter." (Fig 3 caption, p.6). Voting rule, Eq 1-2: Score(a) = sum over verification states v of w_v * #{i | a_i = a and v_i = v}; Output = argmax_a Score(a). Worked example, Fig 4: answer "2" has 3 True, 1 Uncertain, 0 False, so 1x3+0.5x1+0.2x0 = 3.5; answer "5" has 1 True, 1 Uncertain, 4 False, so 2.3. Plain majority picks 5 (6 votes vs 4); weighted voting picks 2.
Verification snippet from Fig 3b: `verification = 1e8 / (smallest_integer ** 4) < 1` returned False for 100, and the model moved to 101 (the underscore is likely an extraction artifact).

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p.3): the same GCD/LCM problem under no-code, code-once and basic prompts. Fig 2 (p.5): accuracy by prompt and level against code usage. Fig 3 (p.6): worked CSV catch, 100 fails the check, 101 passes; the clearest illustration of the loop. Fig 4 (p.8): weighted-voting pipeline with the 3.5 vs 2.3 example. Fig 5 (p.9): accuracy against code usage frequency. Fig 6 (p.11): precision/recall and weight ablation. Figs 7-8: MMLU per-subject charts.

PROBLEMS: Table 1 shows Number Theory +7.6 while Table 4 shows +8.4 for the same 77.2 to 85.6 (the difference is 8.4, so Table 1 is the printed error). Table 4's NL row run together in extraction ("69.29+2.5"). Fig 2a values (60.80, 67.58, 69.94, 74.48) are mapped to prompts by order only. Table 1 lists GPT-4 at 42.20 with no per-subject values. No instructions embedded in the PDF.
